mainTopic: ברכת כהנים: the end of the משנה and the ברייתות that teach how, where, and to whom the כהנים bless
overview: This amud opens at the end of a משנה. In the מקדש the כהנים say ה׳'s Name as it is written and raise their hands above their heads. Outside the מקדש they use a substitute name and raise their hands only to shoulder height. The משנה and רבי יהודה disagree about whether the כהן גדול raises his hands above the ציץ. The גמרא then brings a series of ברייתות, each learning a rule of ברכת כהנים from the words "כה תברכו": it is said in לשון הקודש, standing, with raised hands, and with the שם המפורש, which is used only in the בית המקדש. Along the way רבי יהודה, רבי נתן and רבי יאשיה offer other sources, and רבי נתן answers רבי יונתן's challenge to the proof from אהרן. From "אמור להם" the ברייתות learn that every Jew receives the blessing, and that the כהנים face the people and speak out loud. The amud ends with traditions from אביי and רב חסדא about calling the כהנים up to bless. רב חסדא's explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.title: How the Name is said: in the Temple vs. outside
steps.stepSummary: The משנה finishes its rule. In the מקדש the כהנים say ה׳'s Name as it is written, and outside the מקדש they use a substitute name.
steps.simpleTranslation: [In the Temple they say the Name] as it is written, and in the country they say it with its substitute name.
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining the משנה in the middle of a sentence. It finishes the rule about how the כהנים pronounce ה׳'s Name during ברכת כהנים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה contrasts two places. In the מקדש the כהנים say the שם המפורש exactly as it is spelled. Everywhere else ("מדינה") they say a כינוי, the name we normally use when reading.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written, meaning ה׳'s actual Name, pronounced as spelled
The country, meaning anywhere outside the מקדש
A substitute name used in place of ה׳'s actual Name

phrases.english: as it is written,
phrases.notes: This sentence started on the previous page: in the מקדש the כהנים say ה׳'s Name this way.

phrases.english: and in the country, with its substitute name.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּכְתָבוֹ, וּבַמְּדִינָה בְּכִינּוּיוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a משנה that began on the previous daf
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the מקדש the Name is pronounced as written, and outside it a substitute name is used.

steps.title: How high the priests lift their hands
steps.stepSummary: Outside the מקדש the כהנים lift their hands to shoulder height, and in the מקדש above their heads. The exception is the כהן גדול, who does not lift his hands above the ציץ.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the country, the priests lift their hands opposite their shoulders, and in the Temple above their heads, except for the High Priest, who does not raise his hands above the frontplate.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second difference between the מקדש and everywhere else: how high the כהנים raise their hands during the blessing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just like the Name, the hand-raising is more intense in the מקדש. The כהן גדול is an exception, because he wears the ציץ on his forehead and does not raise his hands above it.

keyTerms.meaning: Lift their hands, as the כהנים do during the blessing
The gold frontplate worn on the כהן גדול's forehead

phrases.english: In the country, the priests lift their hands
opposite their shoulders,
and in the Temple, above their heads.
except for the High Priest,
who does not raise his hands
above the frontplate.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּמְּדִינָה כֹּהֲנִים נוֹשְׂאִים אֶת יְדֵיהֶן כְּנֶגֶד כִּתְפֵיהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second מקדש-vs-outside difference, plus an exception
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Shoulder height outside, above the head in the מקדש. The כהן גדול does not go above the ציץ.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: even the High Priest raises his hands high
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה disagrees with the exception. He holds that the כהן גדול also raises his hands above the ציץ, and he brings a פסוק about אהרן as proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: Even the כהן גדול raises his hands above the ציץ, as it is said: "And אהרן lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה argues on the last part of the משנה. He says the כהן גדול is not an exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His proof is that אהרן, the first כהן גדול, "lifted his hands" to bless the people. רבי יהודה reads this as full lifting, the same as every כהן does in the מקדש, even with the ציץ on.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (introducing a פסוק)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
Even the High Priest raises his hands
above the frontplate,
as it is said: "And Aaron lifted his hands
toward the people and blessed them."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אַף כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל מַגְבִּיהַּ יָדָיו לְמַעְלָה מִן הַצִּיץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disputes the כהן גדול exception
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The כהן גדול also raises his hands above the ציץ, as learned from אהרן.

steps.title: A ברייתא: the blessing must be in the holy tongue
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins with a ברייתא teaching that "כה תברכו" means ברכת כהנים must be said in לשון הקודש.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא. The Sages taught: "So shall you bless" means in the holy tongue.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts and brings a ברייתא that explains the משנה's rule that ברכת כהנים is said only in Hebrew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא first states its rule: the words "כה תברכו" require Hebrew. The next lines will ask why and then give the source.

keyTerms.meaning: So shall you bless, the opening words of ברכת כהנים in the Torah

phrases.english: Gemara
The Sages taught:
"So shall you bless" — in the holy tongue.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: כֹּה תְבָרְכוּ בִּלְשׁוֹן הַקּוֹדֶשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא with a source for the משנה's rule about language
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ברכת כהנים must be said in לשון הקודש.

steps.title: Maybe any language works?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks itself whether the blessing really must be in Hebrew, or whether any language is fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do you say it must be in the holy tongue, or perhaps it may be in any language?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא raises the other possibility so that it can prove its rule. This sets up the next step, the proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing in the words "כה תברכו" plainly says "Hebrew," so one might think any language is fine. The ברייתא asks this to show that a source is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Do you say (the ברייתא questioning its own rule)

phrases.english: Do you say in the holy tongue,
or perhaps it may be in any language?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר בִּלְשׁוֹן הַקּוֹדֶשׁ, אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּכׇל לָשׁוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the rule just stated, to set up its proof
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is Hebrew truly required, or would any language be acceptable?

steps.title: Proof from the blessings at Mount Gerizim
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers with a גזרה שוה. "Bless" appears in ברכת כהנים and also in the blessings at הר גריזים. Just as those were in Hebrew, so is ברכת כהנים.
steps.simpleTranslation: It says here "So shall you bless," and it says there "These shall stand to bless the people." Just as there it was in the holy tongue, so too here it is in the holy tongue.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא proves its rule by linking two פסוקים that both use the word "bless."
steps.deeperAnalysis: The blessings and curses at הר גריזים were already known to be said in Hebrew. The shared word "bless" creates a גזרה שוה, so that Hebrew requirement carries over to ברכת כהנים.

keyTerms.meaning: Learning one law from another because the same word appears in both
Just as ... so too (the conclusion of a comparison)

phrases.english: It is said here: "So shall you bless,"
and it is said there:
"These shall stand to bless the people."
phrases.notes: דברים 27:12, about the blessings at הר גריזים.

phrases.english: Just as there it was in the holy tongue,
so too here, in the holy tongue.

steps.triggerLanguage: נֶאֱמַר כָּאן כֹּה תְבָרְכוּ, וְנֶאֱמַר לְהַלָּן אֵלֶּה יַעַמְדוּ לְבָרֵךְ אֶת הָעָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question by giving the source
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזרה שוה from "לברך" at הר גריזים, which was in Hebrew, proves ברכת כהנים must be in Hebrew.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: the word "כה" already teaches it
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says no גזרה שוה is needed. The word "כה" ("thus") means the כהנים must say the blessing in exactly these words.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: It is not necessary. It says "Thus," meaning only when they say it in this language.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה gives a different, simpler source for the same rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions agree that Hebrew is required. They only disagree about where we learn it from. For רבי יהודה, "כה" means "exactly like this," so the Torah's own Hebrew words must be used.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not necessary (the earlier proof is not needed)

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה is not disagreeing about the halacha. Everyone agrees ברכת כהנים must be in Hebrew. He only argues about the source.
steps.whatToRemember: ברכת כהנים must be said in לשון הקודש. The ברייתא's first opinion learns it from a גזרה שוה with הר גריזים, and רבי יהודה learns it from the word "כה."

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says: It is not necessary;
behold, it says "Thus" —
meaning only when they say it in this language.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ, הֲרֵי הוּא אוֹמֵר כֹּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different source that makes the גזרה שוה unnecessary
steps.mimraCoreRuling: "כה" alone requires the exact Hebrew words.

steps.title: Another ברייתא: the blessing is said standing
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא teaches that "כה תברכו" also means the כהנים must bless while standing.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in another ברייתא: "So shall you bless" means while standing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא with a new rule: the כהנים must stand while blessing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא follows the same pattern as the first one: a rule, a question, then a proof. Here the rule is about body position instead of language.

phrases.english: It is taught in another baraita:
"So shall you bless" — while standing.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ: כֹּה תְבָרְכוּ בַּעֲמִידָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a parallel ברייתא about a new detail
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ברכת כהנים must be said standing.

steps.title: Maybe sitting is also fine?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks whether standing is truly required, or whether the blessing may be said even sitting.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do you say while standing, or perhaps even while sitting?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא raises the other possibility to set up its proof in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "כה תברכו" does not openly say "stand," so one could think sitting is allowed. The question shows that a source is needed.

phrases.english: Do you say while standing,
or perhaps even while sitting?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר בַּעֲמִידָה, אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ בִּישִׁיבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the rule just stated, to set up its proof
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is standing required, or may the blessing be said sitting?

steps.title: Proof: "These shall stand to bless"
steps.stepSummary: Using the same גזרה שוה with הר גריזים, the ברייתא proves that the blessing must be said standing, since there they stood to bless.
steps.simpleTranslation: It says here "So shall you bless," and it says there "These shall stand to bless." Just as there it was while standing, so too here it is while standing.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its question with the same comparison it used for the language rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק at הר גריזים openly says "יעמדו" ("they shall stand") to bless. The shared word "bless" carries that standing requirement over to ברכת כהנים.
steps.whatToRemember: One גזרה שוה between "כה תברכו" and "אלה יעמדו לברך" teaches two rules for ברכת כהנים: it is said in Hebrew, and it is said standing.

phrases.english: It is said here: "So shall you bless,"
and it is said there: "These shall stand to bless."
Just as there it was while standing —
so too here, while standing.

steps.triggerLanguage: נֶאֱמַר כָּאן כֹּה תְבָרְכוּ, וְנֶאֱמַר לְהַלָּן אֵלֶּה יַעַמְדוּ לְבָרֵךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about sitting, using the same גזרה שוה as step 6
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: "יעמדו לברך" at הר גריזים shows that blessing is done standing, and the גזרה שוה applies this to ברכת כהנים.

steps.title: רבי נתן: standing is learned from Temple service
steps.stepSummary: רבי נתן says no גזרה שוה is needed to teach standing. The פסוק puts serving and blessing together, so blessing is done standing, just like serving.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי נתן says: It is not necessary to use that comparison, because the פסוק says 'to minister to Him and to bless in His name.' Just as ministering is done standing, blessing is also done standing.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי נתן offers a different, simpler source for the rule that כהנים must stand while blessing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא in step 10 learned standing from הר גריזים. רבי נתן instead uses one פסוק that names serving and blessing side by side. Since the two are paired, the rules of serving, such as standing, carry over to blessing.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not necessary; this other proof is not needed
To minister to Him; to do the Temple service
One who ministers; the כהן doing the service

phrases.english: Rabbi Natan says: It is not necessary,
phrases.notes: He means we don't need the comparison to הר גריזים from the last step.

phrases.english: for it says: "To minister to Him and to bless in His name."
Just as one who ministers does so standing,
so too one who blesses does so standing.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי נָתָן אוֹמֵר: אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ, הֲרֵי הוּא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different source for the standing rule that step 10 learned from הר גריזים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Blessing is paired with service in one פסוק, so it must be done standing, like service.

steps.title: How do we know Temple service is done standing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of רבי נתן's starting point: that service itself must be done standing.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the ministering itself, from where do we know it is done standing?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to check the foundation of רבי נתן's proof. It asks where we learn that Temple service needs standing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי נתן's proof only works if service really must be done standing. Otherwise there is nothing to carry over to blessing. So the גמרא asks for that source.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know it?

phrases.english: And the ministering itself, from where do we know [it is standing]?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמְשָׁרֵת גּוּפֵיהּ מְנָלַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the premise used in step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source showing that Temple service itself must be done standing.

steps.title: The verse says 'to stand to minister'
steps.stepSummary: The source is a פסוק that joins standing to serving: 'to stand to minister'.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'To stand to minister.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק that says outright that serving is done standing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the פסוק says 'to stand to minister', service needs standing. Now רבי נתן's chain is complete: service is standing, and blessing is paired with service, so blessing is standing.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי נתן learns standing in two links: service needs standing ('to stand to minister'), and blessing is paired with service ('to minister to Him and to bless').

phrases.english: As it is written: "To stand to minister."

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב: לַעֲמֹד לְשָׁרֵת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק 'לעמד לשרת' shows that service requires standing.

steps.title: Another teaching: the blessing needs raised hands
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא says that כה תברכו also teaches that ברכת כהנים is said with raised hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is taught in another ברייתא: 'So shall you bless' means with raised hands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that adds another requirement for ברכת כהנים: raising the hands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far כה תברכו taught Hebrew and standing. Now a third rule is added: נשיאות כפים, raising the hands. The ברייתא will next question this and then prove it.

keyTerms.meaning: Raising the hands, the way כהנים lift their hands for the blessing

phrases.english: It is taught in another ברייתא:
"So shall you bless" means with raised hands.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ: כֹּה תְבָרְכוּ בִּנְשִׂיאוּת כַּפַּיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same pattern as step 8 to bring a new requirement from כה תברכו.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ברכת כהנים must be said with raised hands.

steps.title: Must the hands really be raised?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks whether raised hands are truly required, or whether the blessing may be said without them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do you say it must be with raised hands, or perhaps it may be without raised hands?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא questions its own rule. It is setting up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words כה תברכו do not mention hands at all. So the ברייתא asks how we know that hands matter. This is the same question-and-proof pattern used for standing in steps 9 and 10.

keyTerms.meaning: You say; the opening of a ברייתא's self-question

phrases.english: Do you say it must be with raised hands,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא בִּנְשִׂיאוּת כַּפַּיִם?
phrases.english: or perhaps it may be without raised hands?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר בִּנְשִׂיאוּת כַּפַּיִם, אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא בִּנְשִׂיאוּת כַּפַּיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the rule stated in step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether raised hands are required, or whether the blessing is valid without them.

steps.title: Learning raised hands from אהרן's blessing
steps.stepSummary: A גזרה שוה links כה תברכו to the פסוק where אהרן raised his hands and blessed the people. Just as he raised his hands, so must the כהנים.
steps.simpleTranslation: It says here 'so shall you bless,' and it says there 'And אהרן lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them.' Just as there it was with raised hands, so too here it is with raised hands.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא proves the rule by comparing ברכת כהנים to the time אהרן blessed the people with raised hands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both פסוקים use the idea of blessing. Since אהרן blessed with raised hands, the ברייתא applies the same detail to every ברכת כהנים. This comparison will soon be challenged.

phrases.english: It says here: "So shall you bless,"
and it says there:

phrases.aramaic: ״וַיִּשָּׂא אַהֲרֹן אֶת יָדָיו אֶל הָעָם וַיְבָרְכֵם״.
phrases.english: "And Aaron lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them."
Just as there it was with raised hands,
so too here it is with raised hands.

steps.triggerLanguage: נֶאֱמַר כָּאן כֹּה תְבָרְכוּ, וְנֶאֱמַר לְהַלָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15 with a גזרה שוה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזרה שוה to אהרן's blessing in ויקרא 9:22 shows that raised hands are required.

steps.title: רבי יונתן: then copy all the details of אהרן's blessing
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן objects: if we learn from אהרן's blessing, maybe we should also require everything about that day, meaning a כהן גדול, ראש חודש, and a communal offering.
steps.simpleTranslation: This was difficult for רבי יונתן: If so, just as there it was a כהן גדול, on ראש חודש, with a communal offering, then here too it should need a כהן גדול, ראש חודש, and a communal offering!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יונתן challenges the comparison to אהרן. He asks why we copy only the raised hands and not the other details of that event.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אהרן's blessing happened under special conditions: he was a כהן גדול, it was ראש חודש, and it came with communal offerings. If the גזרה שוה copies one detail, it seems it should copy all of them. That would limit ברכת כהנים to rare occasions, which is clearly wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: The first day of the month
A communal offering, brought for the whole people

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יונתן is not saying the halacha really needs a כהן גדול. He is showing that the גזרה שוה proves too much, since it would also bring along those details.

phrases.english: This was difficult for Rabbi Yonatan:
If so, just as there it was a High Priest,
and Rosh Chodesh, and a communal offering,
then here too it should need a High Priest,
and Rosh Chodesh, and a communal offering?

steps.triggerLanguage: קַשְׁיָא לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יוֹנָתָן: אִי מָה לְהַלָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the גזרה שוה of step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The גזרה שוה linking ברכת כהנים to אהרן's blessing in ויקרא 9:22.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the comparison carries over raised hands, it should also carry over the other details of that event, which would wrongly limit ברכת כהנים to a כהן גדול on ראש חודש with a communal offering.

steps.title: רבי נתן: אהרן's sons are compared to him
steps.stepSummary: רבי נתן uses a הקש instead: 'he and his sons' puts the sons on the same level as אהרן. Just as he blessed with raised hands, so do all his sons.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי נתן says: It is not necessary. The פסוק says 'he and his sons all the days,' comparing his sons to him. Just as he blessed with raised hands, so too his sons bless with raised hands.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי נתן gives another source for raised hands, one that avoids רבי יונתן's problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גזרה שוה compares two events, so it may drag in all of the first event's details. A הקש from 'he and his sons' compares people instead: אהרן and his sons. So ordinary כהנים, not only a כהן גדול, follow אהרן's practice of raised hands.

keyTerms.meaning: He and his sons; אהרן and the כהנים after him
Compares, places side by side to share a rule

phrases.english: Rabbi Natan says: It is not necessary,

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵי הוּא אוֹמֵר ״הוּא וּבָנָיו כׇּל הַיָּמִים״,
phrases.english: for it says: "He and his sons all the days."
It compares his sons to him:
just as he blessed with raised hands,
so too his sons bless with raised hands.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי נָתָן אוֹמֵר: אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ, הֲרֵי הוּא אוֹמֵר הוּא וּבָנָיו כׇּל הַיָּמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the challenged גזרה שוה with a הקש, which answers the כהן גדול part of רבי יונתן's question.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replaces the source: a הקש of sons to father instead of a גזרה שוה between two events.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Raised hands come from a comparison to אהרן's special event, which would also bring in a כהן גדול, ראש חודש, and a communal offering.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק compares אהרן's sons to him, so every כהן blesses with raised hands, not only a כהן גדול.

steps.title: 'All the days': not only on special days
steps.stepSummary: The words 'all the days' show the rule applies every day, not only on ראש חודש or with a communal offering.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is written: 'All the days.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי נתן points to the end of the same פסוק to remove the rest of רבי יונתן's problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הקש settled who may bless, meaning any כהן. 'All the days' settles when: every day, not only ראש חודש or a day of communal offerings.

phrases.english: And it is written: "All the days."

steps.triggerLanguage: וּכְתִיב: כׇּל הַיָּמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer from step 18 by dealing with the ראש חודש and communal offering parts of the challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual support: the words 'all the days' remove any limit to special occasions.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Raised hands might be limited to ראש חודש with a communal offering, like אהרן's day.

steps.title: Blessing is linked to service
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'he and his sons' speaks about service, but blessing is linked to service, so it covers blessing too.
steps.simpleTranslation: And blessing is compared to service.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes a gap in רבי נתן's proof: the פסוק he quoted is about service, not about blessing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'He and his sons all the days' appears in a פסוק about serving. Since another פסוק pairs blessing with serving ('to minister to Him and to bless'), what applies to service also applies to blessing. So the הקש of sons to אהרן works for ברכת כהנים.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי נתן's rule for ברכת כהנים: every כהן, every day, blesses standing and with raised hands. Blessing is tied to Temple service, and 'he and his sons all the days' makes the rule apply to all כהנים always.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is why any כהן raises his hands for ברכת כהנים on ordinary days, not only a כהן גדול on special occasions.

phrases.english: And blessing is compared to service.
phrases.notes: This points back to 'to minister to Him and to bless in His name' from step 11.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיתַּקַּשׁ בְּרָכָה לְשֵׁירוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why a פסוק about service can teach a rule for blessing.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Bridging link: a הקש between blessing and service carries the rule over.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק 'he and his sons' is about service, so it might not apply to blessing.
steps.terutzMaskana: Blessing is compared to service, so the rule covers ברכת כהנים too.

steps.title: Another teaching: the blessing uses the explicit Name
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא teaches that ברכת כהנים is said with the שם המפורש.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: 'So you shall bless the children of Israel' means with the explicit Name of ה׳.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא. It says the כהנים bless using ה׳'s special Name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the topic was how the כהנים bless, for example with raised hands. Now a new question opens: which Name of ה׳ they say. The ברייתא states its rule first, and its source, "ושמו את שמי," comes in step 23.

keyTerms.meaning: The explicit Name of ה׳, the four-letter Name said the way it is written

steps.confusionAlert: The שם המפורש is not the usual way we say ה׳'s Name today. It is the four-letter Name said as it is written, which is not done outside the בית המקדש.

phrases.english: And it is taught in another ברייתא:
"So you shall bless the children of Israel"
With the explicit Name.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַנְיָא אִידַּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new ברייתא on the same פסוק, now about which Name of ה׳ is used.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ברכת כהנים is said with the שם המפורש.

steps.title: Maybe a substitute Name is enough
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks whether the blessing might use only a substitute Name.
steps.simpleTranslation: You say it is with the explicit Name. Or maybe it is only with a substitute Name?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא questions its own ruling. It is setting up a proof from a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'כה תברכו' alone do not clearly prove the special Name. Perhaps the כהנים say the כינוי, the usual substitute Name, as people do everywhere else. The ברייתא needs a clearer source.

keyTerms.meaning: You say (opening a test of a ruling)

phrases.english: You say it is with the explicit Name,
Or perhaps it is only with a substitute Name?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר בַּשֵּׁם הַמְפוֹרָשׁ, אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּכִינּוּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the ruling of step 21 by offering another possibility.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the blessing said with the שם המפורש or only with a כינוי?

steps.title: 'My Name' means the Name unique to ה׳
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'ושמו את שמי' proves that the special Name is used.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'And they shall put My Name.' This means My Name that is unique to Me.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers with a פסוק. 'My Name' means ה׳'s own special Name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'שמי', My Name, points to the Name that belongs only to ה׳. A כינוי is used for other things too, but the four-letter Name is used only for ה׳. So the שם המפורש is required.

keyTerms.meaning: And they shall put My Name

phrases.english: The verse states: "And they shall put My Name"
My Name that is unique to Me.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: וְשָׂמוּ אֶת שְׁמִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'שמי' means the Name unique to ה׳, so the שם המפורש is used.

steps.title: Maybe the special Name is used outside the Temple too
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks whether the שם המפורש is used in ברכת כהנים everywhere, even outside the בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: One might think that even outside the בית המקדש it is done this way.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא raises a possibility it will reject. It is setting up a גזרה שוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 23 proved the special Name is used, but did not say where. Maybe every כהן in every town would say it. The ברייתא now limits the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Outlying areas, any place outside the בית המקדש

phrases.english: One might think that even in the outlying areas it is so
phrases.notes: "Outlying areas" here means anywhere outside the בית המקדש.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל אַף בַּגְּבוּלִין כֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how far the ruling of step 23 reaches.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the שם המפורש used in ברכת כהנים outside the בית המקדש too?

steps.title: A word link limits the special Name to the Temple
steps.stepSummary: A גזרה שוה between 'ושמו את שמי' and 'לשום את שמו שם' limits the שם המפורש to the בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here it says 'And they shall put My Name,' and there it says 'to put His Name there.' Just as there it means the בית הבחירה, so too here it means in the בית הבחירה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers with a גזרה שוה. Both פסוקים use the idea of 'putting ה׳'s Name,' so they share the same place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In דברים, 'to put His Name there' describes the place ה׳ will choose, the בית המקדש. Because ברכת כהנים uses the same wording, it is tied to the same place. So the special Name is said only in the בית המקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: It says here... and it says there (the opening of a word link)
Just as there... so too here
The Chosen House, the בית המקדש

phrases.english: It is stated here: "And they shall put My Name,"
And it is stated there: "to put His Name there."
Just as there, it means the Chosen House,
So too here, it is in the Chosen House.

steps.triggerLanguage: נֶאֱמַר כָּאן וְשָׂמוּ אֶת שְׁמִי, וְנֶאֱמַר לְהַלָּן לָשׂוּם אֶת שְׁמוֹ שָׁם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the possibility raised in step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Through a גזרה שוה, the שם המפורש is used only in the בית המקדש.

steps.title: רבי יאשיה offers a different source
steps.stepSummary: רבי יאשיה says the גזרה שוה is not needed and quotes 'בכל המקום אשר אזכיר את שמי אבוא אליך'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יאשיה says: It is not necessary. For the פסוק says: 'In every place where I mention My Name, I will come to you.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יאשיה brings a different פסוק to prove the same rule. The גמרא will now explain how this פסוק proves it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יאשיה agrees the special Name is only for the בית המקדש. He disagrees only about the source. He thinks a direct פסוק teaches it, so no גזרה שוה is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not necessary (there is a simpler source)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoshiya says: It is not necessary,
For it says:
"In every place where I mention My Name
I will come to you."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יֹאשִׁיָּה אוֹמֵר: אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different source for the conclusion of step 25.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The limit of the שם המפורש to the בית המקדש comes from a פסוק in שמות, not from a גזרה שוה.

steps.title: Surely not 'every place'
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק cannot mean that ה׳ comes to every place where His Name is mentioned.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'In every place'? Could you really think that?
steps.whatsHappening: The פסוק is challenged as it is written. Read plainly, it says ה׳ appears anywhere His Name is said, which does not make sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read in order, the פסוק sounds as if the Name may be said anywhere and ה׳ will come there. That cannot be right. This problem sets up a new reading of the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: Could it enter your mind? (meaning: surely not)

phrases.english: "In every place"? Could you think so?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּכׇל מָקוֹם סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the plain reading of the פסוק quoted in step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: The plain reading of 'בכל המקום אשר אזכיר את שמי'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It cannot be that ה׳'s presence comes to every place His Name is mentioned.

steps.title: Reorder the verse: the Name is mentioned where ה׳ comes
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק is read in a different order: where ה׳ comes and blesses, the בית המקדש, there His Name is mentioned.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this פסוק is reordered: 'In every place where I come to you and bless you, there I will mention My Name.' And where do I come to you and bless you? In the בית הבחירה. So there I will mention My Name, in the בית הבחירה.
steps.whatsHappening: The פסוק is rearranged so that it makes sense. Read this way, it teaches that the special Name is said only in the בית המקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The order is flipped: first comes ה׳'s presence, then the mentioning of His Name. Since ה׳'s presence and blessing are found in the בית המקדש, that is the only place the שם המפורש is said. This gives רבי יאשיה the same rule as the גזרה שוה.

keyTerms.meaning: Reordered; the words are read in a different order

steps.whatToRemember: Both the first ברייתא (with a גזרה שוה) and רבי יאשיה (with a reordered פסוק) agree: ברכת כהנים is said with the שם המפורש only in the בית המקדש.

phrases.english: Rather, this verse is reordered:

phrases.aramaic: בְּכׇל מָקוֹם אֲשֶׁר אָבוֹא אֵלֶיךָ וּבֵרַכְתִּיךָ
phrases.english: In every place where I will come to you and bless you,
There I will mention My Name.
And where will I come to you and bless you?
In the Chosen House.
There I will mention My Name:
In the Chosen House.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מִקְרָא זֶה מְסוֹרָס הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the problem of step 27 by reordering the פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the פסוק in a different word order
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק seemed to say ה׳ comes wherever His Name is mentioned.
steps.terutzMaskana: His Name is mentioned where He comes and blesses, which is the בית המקדש.

steps.title: Who is included in the blessing?
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא asks how we know that גרים, נשים, and עבדים משוחררים also receive ברכת כהנים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: 'So you shall bless the sons of Israel.' This teaches only about the sons of Israel. How do we know about converts, women, and freed slaves?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא with a new question: who receives the blessing. It is setting up a proof from the next words of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'בני ישראל' could be read narrowly, as only Jewish men born into the people. The ברייתא asks for a source to include everyone else.

keyTerms.meaning: I have only (this case so far)

phrases.english: It is taught in another ברייתא:
"So you shall bless the sons of Israel,"
I have derived only the sons of Israel.
Converts, women, and freed slaves: from where do we know?

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ: כֹּה תְבָרְכוּ אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, אֵין לִי אֶלָּא בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new ברייתא about who receives the blessing.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the source that גרים, נשים, and עבדים משוחררים receive ברכת כהנים?

steps.title: 'Say to them' means everyone
steps.stepSummary: The words 'אמור להם' include all of the Jewish people in the blessing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'Say to them.' This means to all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers with the next words of the פסוק. 'To them' covers everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'אמור להם' adds a general word, 'them,' after 'בני ישראל.' This extra word widens the group to include גרים, נשים, and עבדים משוחררים. All of them receive ברכת כהנים.
steps.whatToRemember: ברכת כהנים is for every Jew: born Jews, גרים, נשים, and עבדים משוחררים.

phrases.english: The verse states: "Say to them,"
To all of them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: אָמוֹר לָהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'אמור להם' includes everyone: גרים, נשים, and עבדים משוחררים.

steps.title: The כהנים must face the people
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns from "כה תברכו" and "אמור להם" that ברכת כהנים is said face-to-face with the people.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: "So you shall bless" means face-to-face. Maybe it means the כהנים may face the backs of the people's necks? No. The פסוק says "say to them," like a person talking to his friend.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא that teaches the כהנים must face the people when they bless them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא first suggests that the כהנים might be allowed to stand behind the people. It rejects this from "אמור להם": real talking to someone means facing him, so the ברכה must be face-to-face.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק teaches us (this is the proof)
Like a person speaking to his friend

phrases.english: It is taught in another ברייתא:
"So you shall bless" means face-to-face.
Do you say it means face-to-face,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא פָּנִים כְּנֶגֶד עוֹרֶף?
phrases.english: or perhaps it is only face toward the back of the neck?
The פסוק says: "Say to them,"
like a person who speaks to his friend.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ: ״כֹּה תְבָרְכוּ״ — פָּנִים כְּנֶגֶד פָּנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Like step 30, it learns a law from "אמור להם", this time about how the כהנים stand.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ברכת כהנים must be said with the כהנים facing the people.

steps.title: The ברכה must be said out loud
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא learns from "אמור להם" that ברכת כהנים is said in a loud voice, not in a whisper.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: "So you shall bless" means in a loud voice. Maybe it means in a whisper? No. The פסוק says "say to them," like a person talking to his friend.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more ברייתא that teaches the כהנים must say the ברכה out loud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא uses the same proof as step 31 for a new law. When you talk to a friend, he must be able to hear you, so a whisper is not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: Or perhaps it is only (offers another possible reading)

steps.whatToRemember: From the words "אמור להם" we learn three things: every Jew gets the ברכה, the כהנים face the people, and they say it out loud.

phrases.english: It is taught in another ברייתא:
"So you shall bless" means in a loud voice.
Or perhaps it is only in a whisper?
The פסוק says: "Say to them,"
like a person who speaks to his friend.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ: ״כֹּה תְבָרְכוּ״ — בְּקוֹל רָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same proof from "אמור להם", now used for how loud the ברכה must be.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ברכת כהנים must be said in a loud voice.

steps.title: "כהנים" is called out only for two or more
steps.stepSummary: אביי reports a tradition: "כהנים" is called out when there are two כהנים, but for one כהן nobody calls out "כהן".
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: We have a tradition. When there are two כהנים, the caller says "כהנים". When there is one, he does not call out "כהן". The פסוק says "say to them," which means at least two.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a rule about calling the כהנים up to bless: it is only done when there are at least two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "אמור להם" is plural, "to them". So the call to the כהנים only applies to a group of two or more. A single כהן blesses without being called out.

phrases.english: אביי said: We have a tradition:
for two, he calls out "Priests,"
phrases.notes: The person leading the davening calls the כהנים up to bless.

phrases.english: but for one, he does not call out "Priest,"
as it says: "Say to them," meaning to two.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: נָקְטִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another law learned from "אמור להם", now about calling the כהנים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The call "כהנים" is made only when there are at least two כהנים.

steps.title: Only a כהן calls out "כהנים"
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא reports a tradition: a כהן calls out "כהנים", but a ישראל does not. He starts to explain from "אמור להם".
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב חסדא said: We have a tradition. A כהן calls out "כהנים", but a ישראל does not call out "כהנים", as it says "say to them", the saying...
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא gives a second tradition about who may call out "כהנים". His explanation is cut off here and continues on the next part of the daf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the question is not how many כהנים there are, but who does the calling. The rule is that only a כהן calls, not a ישראל. The proof again comes from "אמור להם", and the word "אמירה" begins the explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: A Jew who is not a כהן or לוי

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two traditions: אביי's is about how many כהנים there must be, and רב חסדא's is about who does the calling.

phrases.english: And רב חסדא said: We have a tradition:
a priest calls out "Priests,"
but an Israelite does not call out "Priests,"
as it says: "Say to them," the saying

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: נָקְטִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second tradition about calling out "כהנים", focused on who calls rather than how many כהנים there are.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only a כהן calls out "כהנים"; a ישראל does not.
